Chapter 1: How Innovators Leave Billions.point: 新品失败的根源，是没把客户付费意愿放在产品设计的核心。
Chapter 1: How Innovators Leave Billions.core: But the root of all innovation evil—what billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk would call the set of “first principles”—is the failure to put the customer's willingness to pay for a new product at the very core of product design.
Chapter 1: How Innovators Leave Billions.case: Then a price was slapped on, and Dodge took it to customers to try to sell it. Market performance was a disaster. In 2012, the year it launched, the Dart sold about 25,000 units5—a quarter of the total predicted by market analysts and a number that caused Dow Jones's MarketWatch to call the Dart the year's second biggest new product flop.
Chapter 1: How Innovators Leave Billions.explain: 菲亚特克莱斯勒开发 Dart 时把财务人员踢出流程，反复设计打磨直到工程师满意，最后才贴上价格推给客户。2012 年只卖出约两万五千辆，仅为分析师预测的四分之一，成了当年第二大新品失败。

Chapter 2: Feature Shocks, Minivations,.point: 小创新的问题不是卖不动，而是价格和市场潜力没有吃满。
Chapter 2: Feature Shocks, Minivations,.core: Minivations are products that tap neither a product concept's full market potential nor its full price potential.
Chapter 2: Feature Shocks, Minivations,.caseTitle: 奥迪 Q7 定价偏低
Chapter 2: Feature Shocks, Minivations,.case: Audi's Q7 luxury SUV launched at €55,000 in the first quarter of 2006. Demand turned out to be 80,000 units per year worldwide, but Audi's production capacity was 70,000 units. That data points to an optimal price of €58,000 (to clear 70K units), which would have meant an extra €210,000,000 a year for Audi on those same 70,000 units.
Chapter 2: Feature Shocks, Minivations,.explain: Q7 定价五万五千欧元，全球年需求八万辆，产能只有七万辆。按需求测算，定价五万八千欧元就能卖完全部产能，同样七万辆每年可多收约两亿一千万欧元。卖得好掩盖了定价太低的损失。

Chapter 3: Why Good People Get It Wrong.point: 好产品自然有人买单是迷思，逆袭故事只是例外。
Chapter 3: Why Good People Get It Wrong.core: We all love these stories. But we love them, in part, because they are exceptions to the rule. No one talks about the 95 percent of cases where the exact opposite happened.
Chapter 3: Why Good People Get It Wrong.case: Many critics made fun of the movie Star Wars when it came out, as did director George Lucas's friends and fellow directors (with the singular exception of Steven Spielberg). Nonetheless, it became one of the biggest movie and merchandising blockbusters of all time. The first Harry Potter book was rejected 12 times before one publisher saw hope in J.K. Rowling's manuscript.
Chapter 3: Why Good People Get It Wrong.explain: 星球大战上映时被嘲笑，哈利波特第一部被退稿十二次，最后都大获成功。这类故事让人相信东西好就一定会被认可，但它们之所以被传颂，正因为是例外，大多数结局相反的案例没人提起。

Chapter 4: Have the “Willingness-to-Pay”.point: 动手开发前先谈付费意愿，才知道哪些功能值得做。
Chapter 4: Have the “Willingness-to-Pay”.core: As the Gillette story shows, it is critical to start the conversation with customers about their willingness to pay for your product before you begin building it.
Chapter 4: Have the “Willingness-to-Pay”.case: When the company actually validated this with customers, it turned out customers were only willing to pay for 10 of the 25 features. (These are shown in Figure 4.2.) Of those 10, the Facebook feature ranked seventh in WTP. For customers, the Facebook feature was a nice-to-have, not a must.
Chapter 4: Have the “Willingness-to-Pay”.explain: 一家网络交易平台的团队花了四周多想出二十五个酷功能。CEO 要求先找几百个潜在客户验证，结果客户只愿为其中十个付费，团队看重的 Facebook 功能也只排第七。研发只做这十个，避免了功能堆砌。

Chapter 5: Don't Default to a One-Size-F.point: 做产品时，只该按需求、价值和付费意愿来细分客户。
Chapter 5: Don't Default to a One-Size-F.core: But when it comes to innovation, there is only one right way to segment: by customers' needs, value, and their willingness to pay for a product or service that delivers that value.
Chapter 5: Don't Default to a One-Size-F.case: Consider the case of Mettler Toledo, a $2.5 billion global manufacturer of weighing instruments. The company's industrial customers need scales that can withstand high impact, large temperature fluctuations, and hazardous environments. Laboratories must have scales that are 100 percent accurate. Retailers need scales that are low-cost, capable of printing, and user-friendly. The underlying technology for weighing things is the same. But Mettler Toledo created different scales based on customer segment needs and WTP. Had it manufactured only one scale, it would have built a one-size-fits-none failure.
Chapter 5: Don't Default to a One-Size-F.explain: 同样的称重技术，工业客户要耐冲击、耐温差，实验室要绝对精准，零售商要便宜、能打印、好用。梅特勒托利多按各细分的需求和付费意愿做不同的秤；如果只做一款，就会谁都不满意。

Chapter 6: When Designing Products, Conf.point: 产品配置要为每个细分只放客户愿意付费的功能。
Chapter 6: When Designing Products, Conf.core: Doing product configuration right means you design a product with the right features for a segment—that is, just the features customers are willing to pay for.
Chapter 6: When Designing Products, Conf.caseTitle: 银行 30 款账户砍到 3 款
Chapter 6: When Designing Products, Conf.case: So what happened after the bank shrank its thirty products to three? You might think sales plummeted because customers had far fewer choices. On the contrary, sales skyrocketed. Why? The bank had finally made each product distinct; its sales staff could articulate each product's value; and customers could easily determine which one best fit their needs. Total annual profit increased by 30 percent in the institution's personal banking services unit.
Chapter 6: When Designing Products, Conf.explain: 一家欧洲区域银行有三十种个人账户，客户和销售都分不清该选哪个。按客户需求和付费意愿归成三类后，每款产品价值清晰、销售讲得明白、客户好选，销量大涨，个人银行业务年利润提升三成。

Chapter 7: Go beyond the Price Point.point: 怎么收费比收多少更重要，错的收费模式比错的价格更伤。
Chapter 7: Go beyond the Price Point.core: The TV set distributor learned a harsh lesson: Monetarily, a bad monetization model can be worse than a bad price.
Chapter 7: Go beyond the Price Point.case: A European trucking company found this out soon after signing a three-year contract to distribute a TV manufacturer's goods. The distributor charged the TV set maker a fixed price per TV delivered. Over time the size of the TVs increased exponentially, which meant the distributor couldn't fit as many TVs into each truck as it used to, and thus had to make more truck runs. Costs increased massively, but revenue did not because of the fixed price. Hence, the TV distributor ultimately lost money on the deal.
Chapter 7: Go beyond the Price Point.explain: 一家欧洲物流公司签了三年合同，按每台电视固定收费。电视越做越大，每车装得越来越少，运输趟数和成本大增，收入却按台数锁死，最终亏钱。问题不在单价，而在计费单位和成本脱了钩。

Chapter 8: Price Low for Market Share or.point: 定价前先定清首要目标，因为利润、收入和份额不可兼得。
Chapter 8: Price Low for Market Share or.core: A clear, overriding goal is a prerequisite because different goals can lead to contradictory strategies and actions.
Chapter 8: Price Low for Market Share or.case: Here's an example: Assume you could sell your product at either $10 or $15. Further assume when you sell your product at $10, you get 100 customers, and when you sell it at $15, you get 80 customers. So how should you price your product? Will you take 20 percent fewer customers in return for a 20 percent increase in revenue? Now let's say the cost to make your product is $7. If you sell it at $10, you have a 30 percent margin. If you sell it at $15, you have a greater than 50 percent margin. So which goal do you want now? Is your answer different?
Chapter 8: Price Low for Market Share or.explain: 定价十美元有一百个客户，十五美元有八十个：要客户数就选低价，要收入则高价多两成。再算上七美元成本，高价的利润率超过百分之五十。目标不同答案就不同，所以必须先排出优先级。

Chapter 9: From Hoping to Knowing.point: 商业论证要把价格、价值、销量和成本联动起来建模。
Chapter 9: From Hoping to Knowing.core: Your business case must model the linkages among the four elements of price, value, volume, and cost.
Chapter 9: From Hoping to Knowing.case: Our model revealed a freemium service would greatly cannibalize the firm's low-priced products, which had gainfully served as the entry-level offerings. In no way would the additional number of freemium customers offset the sizable revenue lost from customers switching from the low-priced to the freemium version.
Chapter 9: From Hoping to Knowing.explain: 一家 SaaS 公司的几位高管很想推出免费入门版来吸引大量用户。把价格和销量联动建模后发现，免费版会大量蚕食原本赚钱的低价产品，新增的免费用户远补不上流失的收入，管理层于是放弃了这个方案。

Chapter 10: The Innovation Won't Speak f.point: 功能不等于收益，要用客户听得懂的话讲出好处。
Chapter 10: The Innovation Won't Speak f.core: When communicating the benefit statements, it's easy to fall into the trap of thinking your features are the same thing as the benefits to your customers. They aren't.
Chapter 10: The Innovation Won't Speak f.case: The offer of 20 gigabytes was most likely much more than what a majority of consumers would ever need. But the words “20 gigabytes” certainly did not identify a problem or a solution. Carbonite changed its description to “unlimited storage,” and the message truly resonated. Consumers could say, “With this service, I don't have to worry about running out of online storage space.”
Chapter 10: The Innovation Won't Speak f.explain: 在线备份公司 Carbonite 原来写的是 20GB 存储，普通消费者无法判断这意味着什么。改成无限存储后，客户立刻明白自己不用担心空间不够，转化率随之提升，尽管大多数人实际用量仍不到 20GB。

Chapter 11: Use Behavioral Pricing Tacti.point: 客户并不总是理性，付费意愿也受价格呈现方式影响。
Chapter 11: Use Behavioral Pricing Tacti.core: Behavioral economics springs from this recognition that buyers are not always rational actors. Their willingness to pay (WTP) for your product is not solely based on the value they get from it.
Chapter 11: Use Behavioral Pricing Tacti.case: The experiment divided people into two groups, A and B. The A group was given two choices: $59 for an online-only subscription and $125 for a print-and-online combination. The B group was offered three choices: $59 for online only, $125 for print only, and $125 for the print/online bundle. The $125 print-only option was an anchor. It made The Economist's print/online bundle for group B look like a great deal; the online edition seemed like a freebie, a throw-in. Some 84 percent chose the print/online bundle in group B versus only 32 percent who chose that bundle in group A.
Chapter 11: Use Behavioral Pricing Tacti.explain: 经济学人的实验中，只有两个选项时，选一百二十五美元印刷加网络套餐的人占百分之三十二。加入同价的纯印刷版后，套餐显得像白送网络版，选择比例升到百分之八十四。产品没变，只是多了一个锚。

Chapter 12: Maintain Your Price Integrit.point: 新品卖得不好就下意识降价，等于告诉市场它不值这个价。
Chapter 12: Maintain Your Price Integrit.core: But reducing your price so soon sends an unintended message: that your new offering has less value than you initially communicated.
Chapter 12: Maintain Your Price Integrit.case: BMW did this in 2001. The company traced the reason behind the slow sales of its new 7 Series sedans. It found that European customers thought it was ugly. (Americans did not.) BMW decided to keep the car's price high. If people do not like the car, they will not buy it, even if it is 10 percent cheaper. Instead, BMW reduced its sales targets—not its price—and started working to design a face-lift right away.
Chapter 12: Maintain Your Price Integrit.explain: 2001 年宝马新 7 系销量不佳，查明原因是欧洲客户觉得它难看。宝马判断客户不喜欢外观，便宜一成也不会买，于是维持高价、下调销量目标，并立即着手改款。先找原因再对症下药，守住了价格。

Chapter 13: Learning from the Best.point: 研发要从客户的真实声音出发，而不是内部的想象。
Chapter 13: Learning from the Best.core: He forced R&D to flip it: Start with the true voice of the customer, not the internal view.
Chapter 13: Learning from the Best.case: The $4,300 product provided big process cost savings for customers, despite commanding a price premium of 35 percent above its next-best competitor. The X-zone 5000 became a huge hit. Product sales were 250 percent higher than expected, margins proved far above average, and the company won a German safety award for the product.
Chapter 13: Learning from the Best.explain: 德尔格的团队下到汉堡的下水道访谈检测工人，发现检测仪常被路人踢进水道、雨天报警又看不清听不见。据此设计的 X-zone 5000 比次优对手贵百分之三十五，销量仍比预期高出百分之二百五十。

Chapter 13: Learning from the Best.point: 用变现模式本身解决供需问题，而不是靠行政手段。
Chapter 13: Learning from the Best.core: Instead, they solved it in the most elegant way possible: with a monetization model.
Chapter 13: Learning from the Best.case: Faced with a shortage of drivers to pick up weekend bar patrons just after last call, Uber “messed around with incentives,” says Gurley. The results were surprisingly strong. By offering additional money, they were able to “move supply off the edge” and get more drivers picking up Bostonians at 2 a.m.
Chapter 13: Learning from the Best.explain: 周末酒吧打烊后司机不够，Uber 没有给司机定配额或强制排班，而是试着加钱激励，结果凌晨两点的波士顿多了许多司机。这就是后来的动态加价：用价格同时调节乘客需求和司机供给。

Chapter 14: Implementing the “Designing.point: 变现流程能否落地，取决于高管是否亲自投入。
Chapter 14: Implementing the “Designing.core: When C-level leadership is not committed in body and soul, if monetizing innovation is not one of your top two organizational priorities, and if that is not reflected in C-level involvement, we would advise you not to embark on the journey.
Chapter 14: Implementing the “Designing.case: In the Simon-Kucher & Partners Global Pricing Study we mentioned in Chapter 1, we found that companies in which senior executives led the change to extract full value from new products averaged 33 percent more profit than companies where executives delegated that responsibility.
Chapter 14: Implementing the “Designing.explain: 西蒙顾和的全球定价研究发现，由高管亲自牵头推动新品价值变现的公司，平均利润比把这件事下放的公司高百分之三十三。所以作者建议，高管若不全身心投入，干脆别启动这场变革。
